rich_summary: After hearing the continuing lament for the dead of the Kurukshetra war, grief spreads again through the Kuru household. Gandhari appeals to the sage Vyasa, describing how Dhritarashtra, the widows of the slain princes, Kunti, Draupadi, and Subhadra all remain tormented years after the slaughter. She begs the powerful ascetic to grant them relief by allowing them to see their departed loved ones. Prompted by Vyasa, Kunti then confesses a long‑hidden secret: in her youth the sage Durvasas gave her a mantra to summon gods. Out of curiosity she invoked the Sun god, Surya, who granted her a son—Karna. Fearing dishonor, she abandoned the child in a river and later kept silent even after recognizing him. Vyasa consoles her, declaring she bears no sin and promising that her wish to behold her son will be fulfilled.

highlight_spans.why: The opening lament captures the persistent psychological aftermath of the war and sets the emotional tone of collective grief.
Gandhari’s appeal to Vyasa gathers the suffering of many characters, emphasizing the shared mourning of the Kuru family.
Kunti’s confession about summoning Surya and secretly giving birth to Karna reveals one of the epic’s most pivotal hidden truths.
Vyasa’s philosophical explanation of divine conception and absolution reframes Kunti’s guilt within the cosmic logic of the epic.

top_scenes.scene_text: Blindfolded Gandhari stands before the sage Vyasa with folded hands while grieving queens and widows gather behind her in a dim royal hall.
Young Kunti in a palace chamber invokes the Sun god as the radiant Surya appears half in the sky and half before her in blazing light.
A sorrowful Kunti places her newborn son Karna in a small basket and sets it afloat on a river at dawn.
